q: Mr A approached the therapist for anger management. After Mr A narrated an incident in which he experienced anger, which of the following is the most appropriate way of further questioning at the initial level?
doubt: Exploring feelings first, option (4), is also defensible in a client-centred frame, but anger is already the named feeling, so the trigger question comes first.
who: Counselling skills: open, non-judgemental questioning

concept.t: What made you angry is an open, non-blaming question about the trigger of the anger, the first thing anger work needs to map.
Anger management (for example Raymond Novaco's stress inoculation approach) starts by finding the provoking situations, then the thoughts, body signals and actions that follow.
Skilled interviewers avoid why questions early on: they sound accusing and invite excuses or intellectualising.

wrong.1: A why question; it sounds like an accusation, makes the client defensive and invites justifications rather than a description of the trigger.
wrong.3: A narrow question about the target person only; it misses the situation, thoughts and events that sparked the anger.
wrong.4: Asks about the feeling, but the client has already said it was anger; feelings work usually follows once the trigger is clear.

q:
Which of the following are true for bootstrapping? 
 
 (a) It involves a large number of sub-samples.

 (b) It does not rely on assumptions about the population.

 (c) It is applicable in case of nonmetric data only.

 (d) It is based on sample data only.

 
 Select the correct option
who: Bradley Efron, bootstrap resampling

concept.t: Statements (a), (b) and (d) are true. The bootstrap draws thousands of resamples with replacement from the one observed sample to estimate a statistic's sampling distribution.
The sample stands in for the population, so no assumption such as normality is needed; the spread of the resampled statistics gives the standard error and confidence interval.
It works with any data, including metric (interval and ratio) data such as means, correlations and regression weights.

wrong.1: Misses (d): the bootstrap is built only from the observed sample data, with no outside population values, so (d) is also true.
wrong.2: Includes (c), which is false, since bootstrapping is widely used with metric data; it also leaves out the true (d).
wrong.4: Drops the true (a), the many resamples that define the method, and adds the false (c).

q:
In Torrance Test of Creative Thinking (figural), picture construction activity is scored for which of the following? 
 
 (a) Fluency

 (b) Flexibility

 (c) Originality

 (d) Elaboration

 
 Select the correct option
who: E. Paul Torrance, TTCT Figural scoring

concept.t: In picture construction the child makes only one picture from a given shape, so there is nothing to count for fluency or flexibility; it is scored for originality and elaboration.
E. Paul Torrance's figural test has three activities: picture construction, picture completion and lines or circles. The last two give many responses, so fluency can also be scored there.
Fluency = number of ideas; flexibility = number of categories; originality = statistical rarity; elaboration = amount of added detail.

wrong.1: Fluency and flexibility need many responses to count, but picture construction yields a single drawing, so neither is scored there.
wrong.3: Flexibility counts the categories across many responses; with only one picture it cannot be scored in this activity.
wrong.4: All four are scored across the figural test as a whole, but not in the single-picture construction activity.

q:
Arrange the following in correct sequence of development of emotional expressions: 
 
 (a) Self-conscious emotions emerge but depend on monitoring and encouragement of adults

 (b) Expression of happiness increases while interacting with familiar people

 (c) Anger and happiness increase in frequency and intensity

 (d) Self-conscious emotions are clearly linked to self-evaluation

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Laura Berk, milestones of emotional development

concept.t: (b) first 6 months: happiness is expressed more with familiar people → (c) 7 to 12 months: anger (and fear) rise in frequency and intensity → (a) 18 months to 2 years: self-conscious emotions appear but depend on adult monitoring → (d) early childhood: they become tied to self-evaluation.
Basic emotions come first. Self-conscious emotions (shame, guilt, pride, embarrassment) need a sense of self, which appears in the second year; judging oneself by inner standards comes later.
Self-conscious emotions are first guided by adults' reactions, then by the child's own standards.

wrong.1: Puts adult-dependent self-conscious emotions (a) before the rise in anger (c), but anger intensifies late in the first year, well before self-conscious emotions appear.
wrong.3: Places self-evaluation (d) before the adult-dependent stage (a); children first rely on adults' reactions and only later judge themselves by their own standards.
wrong.4: Starts with rising anger (c), but greater happiness with familiar people (b) appears earlier, in the first six months along with the social smile.

q: Limbic system, basal ganglia and corpus striatum are parts of which section of the brain?
who: Divisions of the brain: telencephalon

concept.t: The telencephalon is the largest part of the forebrain. It contains the cerebral cortex, the limbic system and the basal ganglia, whose main part is the corpus striatum.
Forebrain = telencephalon + diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus). Midbrain = mesencephalon (tectum, tegmentum). Hindbrain = metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) + myelencephalon (medulla).
Limbic system and basal ganglia → telencephalon; thalamus and hypothalamus → diencephalon.

wrong.1: The midbrain (mesencephalon) holds the tectum (superior and inferior colliculi) and the tegmentum with the substantia nigra, not the limbic system or striatum.
wrong.2: The hindbrain holds the medulla, pons and cerebellum, which control vital functions, posture and balance.
wrong.4: The diencephalon is the thalamus and hypothalamus, the other half of the forebrain; the basal ganglia do not sit there.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): Focus group involves an unstructured interview. 
 Reason (R): Focus group involves interaction among participants moderated by the researcher, as a source of data. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: Many methods texts call focus groups semi-structured because the moderator uses a topic guide, which would make A doubtful and favour (4).
who: Focus group method (moderated group interview)

concept.t: True. A focus group is an unstructured interview with a small group (often 6 to 10 people), run by a moderator in a natural, conversational way.
True. The data come from the group interaction: people react to, build on and challenge each other, with the researcher acting as moderator.
R explains A: because the interaction itself is the data, the moderator keeps the format open instead of working through a fixed list of questions.

wrong.2: R is not a side fact; the reliance on free participant interaction is exactly why the focus group interview is left unstructured.
wrong.3: R is true: interaction among participants, guided by a moderator, is the defining source of focus group data.
wrong.4: A is true in the usual definition: the focus group is a nonstructured, natural group interview, not a fixed questionnaire.

q: Psychometric tests of creativity like the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking measure creativity in terms of:
doubt: Because TTCT scores are counted from the responses produced, some texts describe it as a product measure, which would make (2) the answer.
who: E. Paul Torrance; Mel Rhodes' four Ps of creativity

concept.t: Divergent-thinking tests such as the TTCT treat creativity as a thinking process: E. Paul Torrance defined it as sensing problems or gaps, forming and testing ideas, and communicating the results.
Mel Rhodes sorted creativity into person (traits), process (thinking), product (outputs) and press (environment). Psychometric divergent-thinking tests fall under process.
Fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration are indices of the divergent-thinking process, scored from the responses.

wrong.1: The person approach studies traits of creative people, such as openness or life history, using personality inventories and biographical checklists, not divergent-thinking tasks.
wrong.2: The product approach judges finished creative works, for example by expert ratings in Teresa Amabile's consensual assessment technique, rather than measuring thinking skills.
wrong.4: Persuasion is the P added by Dean Keith Simonton: creativity as convincing others that an idea is valuable; tests do not measure it.

q: Which of the following is true about radioimmunological assays?
who: Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson, radioimmunoassay

concept.t: Radioimmunoassay (RIA) measures tiny amounts of hormones and other substances in blood or tissue, using antibodies and radioactively labelled hormone.
Labelled and unlabelled hormone compete to bind a fixed amount of antibody; the more natural hormone in the sample, the less radioactivity is bound, which gives its concentration.
It was developed by Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson; Yalow received the 1977 Nobel Prize for it.

wrong.2: RIA was developed by Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson; Jay Tepperman did not discover it.
wrong.3: Anatomical methods (histology, staining, tract tracing) show structure; RIA is a biochemical method that measures chemical concentrations.
wrong.4: Brain structure is shown by imaging (CT, MRI) or histology; RIA measures hormone levels, not structures.

q: A competent and well-performing female middle-level manager did not consider herself suitable for the position of senior manager, thinking that females are not suitable for such high positions. This is a typical example of which of the following?
doubt: Her self-limiting belief is internal, so it can also be read as low motivation to approach success (2), close to Matina Horner's fear of success.
who: Glass ceiling (gender barrier to top positions)

concept.t: The glass ceiling is an invisible barrier, built on attitudes and stereotypes, that keeps capable women from top posts. Here the stereotype is held by the manager herself, so she rules herself out.
Gender stereotypes that link leadership with men act from outside (biased promotions) and from inside (women doubting they fit); both keep women below senior level.
Glass ceiling = women stuck below the top; glass cliff = women promoted into risky, failing posts.

wrong.2: A low achievement motive (David McClelland, John Atkinson) would show across tasks; she is competent and performing well, and the block comes from a gender stereotype.
wrong.3: Gender discrimination is unfair treatment by others, such as being passed over; here no one has blocked her, she applies the stereotype to herself.
wrong.4: Atkinson's motive to avoid failure is a general fear of failing; her doubt rests on a belief about women, not on fear of failure.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): Tolman's purposive behaviourism was considered to be a major advancement in the field of Psychology. 
 Reason (R): Pre-Tolman behaviourism excessively emphasized S-R relations and ignored cognitive processes. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Edward Tolman, purposive behaviourism

concept.t: True. Edward Tolman kept behaviourist methods but argued that behaviour is purposive (goal-directed) and guided by expectancies and cognitive maps.
True. Earlier behaviourism, led by John B. Watson, reduced behaviour to stimulus-response links and excluded mental processes.
R explains A: Tolman's advance was bringing cognition back through intervening variables, filling the gap left by pure S-R theory. He is seen as a bridge to cognitive psychology.

wrong.2: R is the very reason Tolman mattered: he added the cognitive variables that S-R behaviourism had left out.
wrong.3: R is true: John B. Watson's behaviourism studied only observable stimulus-response links and rejected mental concepts.
wrong.4: A is true: Tolman's latent-learning and cognitive-map studies are seen as a major step towards cognitive psychology.

q:
Which of the following are characteristics of post-trauma growth? 
 
 (a) Relationships are strengthened or enhanced

 (b) Self-views become more positive

 (c) Life philosophies become ambiguous

 (d) Greater acceptance of personal limitations

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun, post-traumatic growth

concept.t: Statements (a), (b) and (d) are true. After trauma many people report closer relationships, a stronger, more positive self-view, and greater acceptance of their own limits and vulnerability.
Growth shows in self-perception (strength plus accepting limits), relationships (closeness, compassion) and life philosophy (new priorities, more appreciation of life, spiritual change).
Life philosophies become clearer, not ambiguous: people rethink their priorities and value life more.

wrong.1: Includes (c), which is false, since philosophy of life becomes clearer and more meaningful; it also drops the true (d).
wrong.3: Includes the false (c) and leaves out (a), the strengthening of relationships, a core area of growth.
wrong.4: Includes the false (c) and leaves out (b), the stronger and more positive self-view people report.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Psychologist): (a) Binet and Simon; (b) Terman; (c) Thorndike; (d) Eysenck M W 
 List-II (Definition): (i) The power of good response from the perspective of truth or fact; (ii) The capacity to judge, understand and reason well; (iii) The capacity to learn concepts and grasp their significance; (iv) Error-free transmission of information through the cortex 
 Select the correct option:
who: Classic definitions of intelligence: Binet, Terman, Thorndike, Eysenck

concept.t: (a) Alfred Binet and Théodore Simon = (ii) to judge, understand and reason well; (b) Lewis Terman = (iii) capacity to learn concepts and grasp their significance; (c) Edward Thorndike = (i) power of good responses from the point of view of truth or fact; (d) Eysenck = (iv) error-free transmission of information through the cortex.
Binet: judgement is the core of intelligence. Terman: abstract thinking. Thorndike: good responses (a connectionist view). Eysenck: a biological, neural-efficiency view.

wrong.1: Gives Binet and Simon the biological definition, which is Eysenck's, and Eysenck their judgement definition; Terman and Thorndike are right.
wrong.2: Gives Binet and Simon Thorndike's 'good responses' definition and Terman the judgement definition; only Eysenck is paired correctly.
wrong.4: Every pair is wrong: for example Thorndike gets Eysenck's neural definition and Eysenck gets Thorndike's 'good responses'.

q: Skills that are operated automatically and without thinking are noted in which memory?
who: Implicit versus explicit memory (Daniel Schacter)

concept.t: Implicit memory shows itself in performance without conscious recollection. Skills that run automatically, such as typing or cycling, are its procedural part.
Implicit (non-declarative) memory covers procedural skills, priming and classical conditioning; it relies on the basal ganglia and cerebellum more than the hippocampus.
Explicit = 'knowing that' (can be put into words); implicit = 'knowing how' (shown by doing).

wrong.2: Explicit (declarative) memory is conscious recall of facts and events, split by Endel Tulving into semantic and episodic memory.
wrong.3: Flashbulb memory (Roger Brown and James Kulik) is a vivid, detailed memory of the moment one heard shocking news.
wrong.4: Autobiographical memory is the conscious record of one's own life events, a kind of explicit, episodic memory.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): According to classical theory of test scores, total variance is equal to true variance plus error variance. 
 Reason (R): Classical theory of test scores assumes a significant but low positive correlation between true scores and error scores. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Classical test theory (true score model)

concept.t: True. In classical test theory X = T + E, so total variance = true variance + error variance (σ2X = σ2T + σ2E).
False. The model assumes errors are random, so the correlation between true scores and error scores is zero, not low positive.
That zero correlation lets the variances add with no covariance term; reliability is then σ2T / σ2X.

wrong.1: R is false: classical theory assumes true and error scores are uncorrelated (r = 0), so it cannot explain A.
wrong.2: R is not true; any correlation between true and error scores would add a covariance term and break the simple variance sum.
wrong.4: A is true: total variance splitting into true plus error variance is the basic equation of classical test theory.

q: What is the term given to 'autonomy, or being self-determining, independent and able to resist social pressures to think and act in certain ways'?
who: Carol Ryff, psychological well-being model (1989)

concept.t: Autonomy (self-determination, independence, resisting social pressure, judging oneself by personal standards) is one of the six dimensions of psychological well-being in Carol Ryff's model.
Self-acceptance, positive relations with others, autonomy, environmental mastery, purpose in life and personal growth.
Ryff's model is eudaimonic (functioning well); Ed Diener's subjective well-being is hedonic (feeling good).

wrong.1: Emotional well-being is the hedonic side: positive feelings, few negative feelings and life satisfaction, as in subjective well-being.
wrong.2: Social well-being (Corey Keyes) covers functioning in society: social integration, contribution, acceptance, actualisation and coherence.
wrong.4: Physical well-being is bodily health and fitness, not a psychological quality such as autonomy.

q:
Which of the following are the behaviours identified by Maslow that lead to self-actualization? 
 
 (a) Growth choices

 (b) Use of ego defence

 (c) Self-awareness

 (d) Concentration

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Abraham Maslow, behaviours leading to self-actualisation

concept.t: Abraham Maslow listed behaviours that lead to self-actualisation; (a) making growth choices, (c) self-awareness and (d) full concentration (experiencing life with total absorption) are among them.
Maslow said we must identify and give up ego defences, not use them, because defences distort reality and block growth.
Being honest and taking responsibility, trusting one's own judgement, developing one's potential and having peak experiences.

wrong.1: Includes (b), but Maslow asked people to give up their ego defences; it also leaves out concentration.
wrong.3: Self-awareness fits but use of ego defence does not; the pair also misses growth choices and concentration.
wrong.4: Includes the use of ego defence, which Maslow saw as a barrier to growth, and leaves out self-awareness.

q: The vicious circles that maintain depression, loneliness and shyness can be broken by social skill training, by positive experience that alters self-perception, by changing negative thought patterns. This is the description of which social-psychological approach to treatment?
doubt: Changing negative thought patterns is the core of explanatory style therapy (2), the other technique in the same 'breaking vicious cycles' approach, so (2) is the runner-up.
who: David Myers, breaking vicious cycles in treatment

concept.t: The description is David Myers' 'breaking vicious cycles' approach, and social skills training is its main tool: practised skills bring social success, and that success changes how people see themselves.

Depressed, lonely and shy people act in ways that bring rejection, which confirms their negative self-image. Social skills training and explanatory style therapy (changing negative attributions) break this loop.
Myers' approaches: changing behaviour to change inner states, breaking vicious cycles, keeping gains through internal attributions, and therapy as social influence.

wrong.2: Explanatory style therapy covers only the thinking strand: it retrains self-blaming, stable, global explanations of failure.
wrong.3: Internal attribution is how change is maintained: people keep improvements when they credit them to their own effort rather than to the treatment.
wrong.4: Social influence is the view that therapy works partly through persuasion by a credible therapist, not the vicious-cycle approach described.

q: Which of the following is a step to transformative change in which an unpredictable and often affective experience occurs?
who: Organic inquiry, transpersonal research method (Jennifer Clements)

concept.t: In organic inquiry, change happens in three steps; the middle step, inspiration, is the unpredictable, often emotional experience in which new insight breaks through.
Preparation (immersing in the topic) → inspiration (the unplanned, affective breakthrough) → integration (making sense of it and letting it change the person).
Organic inquiry is a qualitative, transpersonal research approach in which the personal transformation of researcher and participants is part of the findings.

wrong.1: Integration is the final step, when the insight is understood and absorbed into daily life; it is reflective rather than sudden.
wrong.2: Preparation is the first, deliberate step of getting ready and immersing in the topic, before any unplanned experience occurs.
wrong.4: Organic inquiry is the name of the whole research method, not one of its steps.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): Clients must be allowed complete freedom to discuss in their natural manner to communicate respect and acceptance. 
 Reason (R): Completely suspending judgement and expressing positive regard are Rogers' core therapeutic conditions. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: R names only part of Rogers' three core conditions (it leaves out congruence and empathy), so some would treat it as incomplete and prefer (2).
who: Carl Rogers, client-centred therapy core conditions

concept.t: True. In client-centred therapy the client leads and talks in their own way; letting them do so shows respect and acceptance.
True in substance. Suspending judgement while valuing the client is unconditional positive regard, one of Carl Rogers' core conditions with empathy and congruence.
R explains A: the freedom given to the client is how the therapist expresses non-judgemental, unconditional positive regard.

wrong.2: R is the basis of A: allowing free expression is how the therapist puts non-judgemental positive regard into practice.
wrong.3: R is true: unconditional positive regard means accepting the client without judgement, and it is one of Rogers' core conditions.
wrong.4: A is true: client-centred therapy is non-directive, so the client is free to explore in their own way.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Concept): (a) Reward power; (b) Coercive power; (c) Referent power; (d) Legitimate power 
 List-II (Description): (i) Potential to deliver threats and punishment to others; (ii) Authority of a person by virtue of certain characteristics; (iii) Positive reinforcement to produce change; (iv) Power to influence others 
 Select the correct option:
who: John French and Bertram Raven, bases of social power (1959)

concept.t: (a) Reward power = (iii) positive reinforcement to produce change; (b) Coercive power = (i) threats and punishment; (c) Referent power = (iv) power to influence others through liking and identification; (d) Legitimate power = (ii) authority held by virtue of certain characteristics such as role or position.
John French and Bertram Raven named five bases of power: reward, coercive, legitimate, referent and expert; Raven later added informational power.
Reward and coercion work through consequences; legitimate power through accepted authority; referent power through people wanting to be like the leader.

wrong.1: Gives coercive power the authority description and legitimate power the threats description; coercion is about punishment, legitimacy about recognised authority.
wrong.2: Shifts every pair: reward power is giving positive reinforcement, not general influence, and coercive power is threats, not reinforcement.
wrong.4: Gives reward power the punishment description; rewards are positive reinforcement, while threats and punishment define coercive power.

q: Which of the following explains the theory's ability to organize and explain several otherwise disjointed observations?
who: B. R. Hergenhahn, functions of scientific theory

concept.t: A theory's synthesising function is its power to organise and explain many observations that would otherwise stand apart, tying them into one framework.
B. R. Hergenhahn describes two functions of a scientific theory: the synthesising function (organising known facts) and the heuristic function (generating new research).
Synthesising looks back, organising old facts; heuristic looks forward, prompting new studies.

wrong.1: The heuristic function is a theory's ability to generate new research and hypotheses, guiding future observation rather than organising existing ones.
wrong.3: The principle of verification, from logical positivism, says a statement is meaningful only if it can be checked by observation.
wrong.4: Not a named function of theory; the two standard functions are synthesising and heuristic.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): According to Rogers, all people are capable of growth and personal development. 
 Reason (R): Positive change is a natural and expected progression. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Carl Rogers, actualising tendency

concept.t: True. Carl Rogers held that every person has the capacity for growth, self-direction and personal development.
True. Rogers saw positive change as natural because of the actualising tendency, an inborn drive to develop one's potential.
R explains A: people can grow because growth is the natural, expected course once the right conditions (genuineness, unconditional positive regard, empathy) are present.

wrong.2: R is the reason behind A: the actualising tendency makes positive change natural, which is why everyone is seen as capable of growth.
wrong.3: R is true: for Rogers, growth is the natural direction of the organism, blocked only by conditions of worth.
wrong.4: A is true: Rogers' view of human nature is optimistic, holding that everyone can grow and develop.

q: Jung identified eight personality types on the basis of which of the following?
who: Carl Jung, psychological types

concept.t: Carl Jung crossed two attitudes (extraversion, introversion) with four functions (thinking, feeling, sensing, intuiting), giving 2 × 4 = 8 types.
Thinking and feeling are rational (judging) functions; sensing and intuiting are irrational (perceiving). An extraverted thinking type, for example, turns logical judgement outward.
The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator built on Jung's types by adding a judging-perceiving dimension, giving 16 types.

wrong.2: Reverses the numbers: Jung described only two attitudes (extraversion, introversion) and four functions.
wrong.3: Four by four would give 16 types, the Myers-Briggs number; Jung's model has only two attitudes.
wrong.4: Jung named four functions, not six; two attitudes by six functions would give 12 types, not eight.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): If all the assumptions are fulfilled, addition of any predictor in the Multiple Regression Analysis will increase the value of the coefficient of determination. 
 Reason (R): Correlation of the criterion variable with the predictor variables can be positive or negative. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: Strictly, R squared stays unchanged when a new predictor adds no unique variance, so A could be judged false, favouring (4), whose printed wording looks like a misprint.
who: Multiple regression: coefficient of determination (R squared)

concept.t: True in the usual sense. Adding a predictor can never lower R2; it rises by the new predictor's squared semipartial correlation, which cannot be negative.
True. A predictor can relate to the criterion positively or negatively; the sign only sets the sign of its regression weight.
R does not explain A: R2 grows because explained variance cannot shrink when a variable is added, whatever the sign. This is why adjusted R2 is used to penalise extra predictors.

wrong.1: The sign of the correlation does not drive the rise in R squared; an added predictor adds non-negative explained variance whether it correlates positively or negatively.
wrong.3: R is true: criterion-predictor correlations can be positive or negative, and both kinds contribute to prediction.
wrong.4: A is true in the usual sense, since R squared never falls when a predictor is added, and R is true, not false.

q: A 30-year-old man identified as Mr K C suffered a serious motorcycle accident. Mr K C remembers many things but cannot remember everything. Mr K C seems to have which memory loss?
who: Endel Tulving, patient K.C. (episodic amnesia)

concept.t: K.C., studied by Endel Tulving, lost his episodic memory after a motorcycle accident: he could recall no personal events from his life, yet kept his general knowledge.
Episodic memory stores personally experienced events tied to a time and place ('my last birthday'); semantic memory stores facts and word meanings ('Paris is in France').
K.C. is the classic case showing that episodic and semantic memory are separate systems.

wrong.1: K.C.'s semantic memory (facts, language, general knowledge) stayed largely intact; what he lost was memory for his own experiences.
wrong.3: Procedural memory (skills such as playing cards or riding a bicycle) was spared in K.C., as in most amnesic patients.
wrong.4: Working memory, the short-term workspace for holding and handling information, was largely normal in K.C.; his loss was long-term recall of personal episodes.

q: While conducting an experiment, the researcher manipulates the independent variable within a pre-decided range. Which of the following describes this type of research?
who: Fixed versus random effects in ANOVA

concept.t: In a fixed effect model the researcher deliberately chooses the levels of the independent variable in advance (for example 0, 10 and 20 mg), so conclusions apply only to those levels.
In a random effect model the levels are drawn at random from a larger population of possible levels, so the results generalise to all levels.
Levels picked by the experimenter = fixed; levels sampled by chance = random; a design with both kinds of factor = mixed model.

wrong.1: Lacks random assignment of participants, usually because it uses pre-existing groups; it says nothing about how the levels of the independent variable are chosen.
wrong.2: Here the levels of a factor are a random sample from a wider population of levels, not a range the researcher fixes in advance.
wrong.4: Combines quantitative and qualitative data collection in one study; it is not about choosing levels of an independent variable.

q:
Consideration of mental health needs of a person with cancer will have positive effects on: 
 
 (a) Quality of life

 (b) Emotional well-being

 (c) Positive biological changes

 (d) Killing carcinogenic cells

 
 Select the correct option:
doubt: Evidence that psychological care produces biological change is suggestive rather than settled, so a cautious reading gives (1), quality of life and emotional well-being only.
who: Psycho-oncology and psychoneuroimmunology

concept.t: Caring for the mental health of a person with cancer improves quality of life and emotional well-being, and lowering stress can bring positive biological changes, such as healthier stress-hormone and immune functioning.
Psychoneuroimmunology studies how stress acts on the immune system through the HPA axis and cortisol; reducing stress and depression helps the body's regulatory systems.
Psychological care does not directly kill cancer cells; that is the job of surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and other medical treatment.

wrong.1: Leaves out (c): reducing stress and depression in people with cancer is linked to measurable bodily gains, such as healthier cortisol rhythms and immune function.
wrong.2: Leaves out the clearest benefits, (a) and (b), and includes (d), which is false because psychological care does not destroy cancer cells.
wrong.4: Includes (d), which is false, and leaves out (a), quality of life, the best-documented benefit of psychological care in cancer.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): In simple regression analysis, if the value of one regression coefficient (bxy) is less than 1.00, the value of the second regression coefficient (byx) has to be less than 1.00. 
 Reason (R): The correlation between two variables x and y is equal to the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients (bxy and byx). 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Properties of regression coefficients

concept.t: False. Because r2 = bxy × byx and r2 cannot exceed 1, both coefficients cannot be greater than 1; but if one is below 1 the other can still exceed 1 (0.5 × 1.6 gives r2 = 0.8).
True. The correlation coefficient is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients: r = √(bxy × byx), taking the common sign of the two.
If one regression coefficient is more than 1, the other must be less than 1; the reverse does not hold.

wrong.1: (A) is false, so (R) cannot explain it; the geometric-mean rule only forbids both coefficients from exceeding 1 at the same time.
wrong.2: (A) is false: one coefficient below 1 does not force the other below 1, since 0.5 and 1.6 give a valid r<sup>2</sup> of 0.8.
wrong.3: Reverses the truth: (R) is the true statement, r = √(b<sub>xy</sub> × b<sub>yx</sub>), and (A) is the false one.

q: Which one of the following is the correct answer for the experiment conducted at the University of California at Santa Barbara, in which individuals running on a jogging path speeded up as they came upon a woman seated on the grass facing them rather than sitting with her back turned?
who: Charles Worringham and David Messick, jogging-path study

concept.t: Joggers sped up only when the woman faced them and could watch them, not when her back was turned; her presence was the same, so the boost came from concern about being evaluated.
Evaluation apprehension (Nickolas Cottrell) holds that others arouse us because we worry about how they will judge us, and this arousal strengthens dominant, well-learned responses such as running.
Robert Zajonc = mere presence arousal; Cottrell = evaluation apprehension; Robert Baron = distraction-conflict.

wrong.1: Robert Baron's distraction-conflict theory says an audience splits attention between task and observers; it does not explain why facing versus turning away made the difference.
wrong.2: Means someone doing the same task alongside you, as in Norman Triplett's racing cyclists; the woman was sitting on the grass, not jogging.
wrong.4: Group members who slack off and benefit from others' effort, a feature of social loafing when individual output cannot be identified.

q: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of attention?
who: Features of attention: capacity, selectivity, control, automaticity

concept.t: Initial detection of stimuli is the job of sensation, the receptors registering energy from the world; attention works on that input afterwards by selecting what gets further processing.
Attention has limited processing capacity, so it must be selective; it can be steered under voluntary control; and well-practised tasks become automatic, needing little attention.
Sensation = detecting; perception = interpreting; attention = selecting and focusing limited mental resources.

wrong.1: Fits: attention is a limited-capacity resource, so it must select some inputs and ignore others, as Donald Broadbent's filter model proposed.
wrong.2: Fits: practised tasks run with little attentional effort; Walter Schneider and Richard Shiffrin contrasted such automatic processing with effortful controlled processing.
wrong.4: Fits: attention can be directed voluntarily (top-down) or captured by salient stimuli (bottom-up), so control of attention is a core feature.

q: What is the theoretical approach called which attempts to explain completely the phenomenon of one field of study in terms of the dynamics of a more basic field?
who: Reductionism, philosophy of science

concept.t: Reductionism explains a phenomenon completely in terms of a more basic field, for example explaining depression entirely by neurotransmitters, or behaviour entirely by physiology.

Psychology is reduced to biology, biology to chemistry, chemistry to physics; critics reply that whole systems show emergent properties their parts lack, the Gestalt point that the whole differs from the sum of its parts.

wrong.1: Holds that two factors, such as mind and body or person and situation, influence each other; it does not reduce one field to another.
wrong.3: The philosophy of William James and John Dewey that judges ideas by their practical consequences and usefulness.
wrong.4: Karen Horney's compliant (self-effacing) solution is a neurotic trend of moving toward people to win love and approval; it is not a theory of explanation.

q: According to Adler, which of the following is used by the neurotic to escape from problems?
doubt: Some keys may pick (4), the umbrella term, since all three kinds are safeguarding strategies; but the one that is itself an escape from problems is distancing.
who: Alfred Adler, safeguarding through distance

concept.t: Alfred Adler said neurotics escape life's tasks (work, love, friendship) by keeping a distance from them. He called this withdrawal, or safeguarding through distance.
Moving backward (retreating to a safer, younger way of living), standing still (not moving at all), hesitating (putting things off) and constructing obstacles (a small barrier to blame).
Distancing is one of three safeguarding tendencies that protect a fragile self-esteem: excuses ('Yes, but'), aggression (depreciation, accusation, self-accusation) and withdrawal.

wrong.1: Belittling others and overvaluing oneself; an aggressive safeguarding tendency that attacks people, not one that escapes problems.
wrong.2: Using guilt and self-torment to hurt the people close to you; another aggressive safeguarding tendency, not a way of escaping.
wrong.4: The umbrella term for all three kinds (excuses, aggression, withdrawal); they protect self-esteem, and the one that escapes problems is distancing.

q:
Which among the following are the assumptions on which Binet developed his first test of intelligence? 
 
 (a) Mental competence increases over the childhood years

 (b) A child's relative standing in mental development compared to his age group will remain constant as the child grows.

 (c) A child's relative standing in mental development compared to his age group increases as the child grows

 (d) Mental competence decreases over the childhood years

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon, Binet-Simon scale

concept.t: Alfred Binet assumed that mental competence grows through childhood, so tasks could be graded by the age at which most children pass them, and that a child's relative standing among age-mates stays roughly constant.
These assumptions gave the idea of mental age: a child who passes the items typical of 10-year-olds has a mental age of 10, whatever the chronological age.
Constant relative standing later underpinned William Stern's ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100), which stays stable only if a child keeps the same position.

wrong.2: Statement (c) is false: if relative standing kept rising, mental age would not give a stable index of how a child compares with peers.
wrong.3: Leaves out (a), the core assumption that mental competence increases with age, and includes the false statement (c).
wrong.4: Statement (d) contradicts the age-scale idea: Binet's items are graded precisely because competence increases, not decreases, across childhood.

q: On a Wechsler-type Adult Intelligence Scale, having normally distributed scores, a subject had a percentile rank of 84. His deviation IQ would be:
who: David Wechsler's deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15

concept.t: On a normal curve about 84% of scores fall below +1 SD (50% below the mean plus 34% between the mean and +1 SD). Wechsler scales use mean 100 and SD 15, so IQ = 100 + 15 = 115.
z = (IQ - 100) / 15. Percentile 84 gives z = +1, so IQ = 100 + (1 × 15) = 115.
Percentiles 16, 50, 84 and 98 match Wechsler IQs of about 85, 100, 115 and 130.

wrong.1: Confuses the percentile rank with the IQ; a percentile is the percentage of people scoring below a person, not a point on the IQ scale.
wrong.2: That IQ is 1 SD below the mean, which corresponds to the 16th percentile, not the 84th.
wrong.4: That IQ is about 1.33 SD above the mean, roughly the 91st percentile.

q: According to self-determination theory, which of the following form the basis of intrinsic motivation?
who: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, self-determination theory

concept.t: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan argue that intrinsic motivation rests on feeling competent (effective) and autonomous (self-directed); rewards that undermine either feeling reduce it.
Self-determination theory names three basic psychological needs: competence, autonomy and relatedness; relatedness supports intrinsic motivation, but competence with autonomy is its core.
Controlling rewards lower intrinsic motivation (the overjustification effect); informative feedback that raises felt competence increases it.

wrong.1: Only half right: experience is not one of Deci and Ryan's basic needs, which are competence, autonomy and relatedness.
wrong.3: Only half right: novelty seeking is a temperament dimension in Robert Cloninger's model, not a basic need in self-determination theory.
wrong.4: Both are personality traits, novelty seeking from Robert Cloninger and sensation seeking from Marvin Zuckerman; neither is a basic need in self-determination theory.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Concept): (a) Naturalistic intelligence; (b) Cognitive processing speed; (c) Meta-components; (d) Motivating oneself 
 List-II (Description): (i) Skill critical and important for archaeologists and botanists; (ii) Ability to execute easy and highly overlearned cognitive tasks; (iii) Mental processes individuals use effectively to guide their problem-solving efforts; (iv) Delaying gratification and stifling impulsiveness 
 Select the correct option:
who: Howard Gardner, Robert Sternberg, Daniel Goleman; CHC processing speed

concept.t: (a) Naturalistic intelligence = (i) skill for archaeologists and botanists; (b) Cognitive processing speed = (ii) executing easy, overlearned tasks; (c) Meta-components = (iii) processes that guide problem-solving; (d) Motivating oneself = (iv) delaying gratification, stifling impulsiveness.
Naturalistic intelligence (recognising and classifying living things) is Howard Gardner's eighth intelligence; processing speed (Gs) is a broad ability in the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model.
Meta-components are the executive planning and monitoring processes in Robert Sternberg's componential subtheory; motivating oneself is a domain of Daniel Goleman's emotional intelligence.

wrong.2: Swaps (a) and (b), and (c) and (d): fluent execution of overlearned tasks is processing speed, and delaying gratification belongs to motivating oneself.
wrong.3: Gives meta-components to the botanist's skill and motivating oneself to overlearned tasks; meta-components guide problem-solving and self-motivation means delaying gratification.
wrong.4: Reverses every pair; for instance, delaying gratification belongs to motivating oneself, not to naturalistic intelligence.

q:
Which of the following is/are true about rhodopsin? 
 
 (a) It is a rod pigment that enables vision in low light

 (b) It is a cone pigment that enables vision in bright light

 (c) It is a G-protein coupled receptor

 (d) It is a cone pigment and G-protein coupled receptor.

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Rhodopsin, the rod photopigment

concept.t: Rhodopsin is the photopigment in rods, which give sensitive, colourless vision in dim light; it is also a G-protein coupled receptor, so (a) and (c) are true.
Light changes the retinal (a vitamin A derivative) inside rhodopsin, which activates the G-protein transducin; this closes sodium channels and hyperpolarises the rod.
Rods = rhodopsin, scotopic (night) vision; cones = three photopsins, photopic colour vision.

wrong.1: True but incomplete: rhodopsin is also a G-protein coupled receptor, so (c) is true as well.
wrong.2: Includes (d), which is false: rhodopsin is found in rods, not cones; cones use their own opsins.
wrong.3: Statement (b) is false: bright-light colour vision depends on cone pigments (photopsins), while rhodopsin is bleached in bright light.

q: Mrs B has attained the level of 'self' in that she now takes genuine pleasure in praying, meditation and other spiritual activities. Which type of 'self' is this in Sufism?
who: Robert Frager, Sufi seven levels of the self (nafs)

concept.t: In Sufism the Inspired Self (nafs mulhima) is the stage where a person first takes genuine pleasure in prayer, meditation and other spiritual practices, rather than doing them only out of duty.
Seven levels of nafs: Tyrannical (ammara), Regretful (lawwama), Inspired (mulhima), Serene (mutma'inna), Pleased (radiya), Pleasing to God (mardiyya), Pure (safiya).
Regretful = first insight into one's faults; Inspired = joy in spiritual practice; Serene = inner peace; Pure = the ego dissolved in union with God.

wrong.1: The fourth level (nafs mutma'inna), after the Inspired Self; its mark is deep inner peace and contentment.
wrong.3: The fifth level (nafs radiya), content with whatever God sends, hardship included, not simply delighting in spiritual practice.
wrong.4: The seventh and highest level (nafs safiya), where the ego has dissolved and the person lives in full unity with God.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Concept): (a) Mental representation; (b) Operations; (c) Adaptation; (d) Assimilation 
 List-II (Explanation): (i) Building schemas through direct interaction with the environment; (ii) Using current schemas to interpret the external world; (iii) The ability to remember and copy the behaviour of models who are not present; (iv) Mental representation of actions that obey logical rules 
 Select the correct option:
who: Jean Piaget's cognitive-developmental theory

concept.t: (a) Mental representation = (iii) remembering and copying absent models (deferred imitation); (b) Operations = (iv) mental actions that obey logical rules; (c) Adaptation = (i) building schemas through direct interaction with the environment; (d) Assimilation = (ii) using current schemas to interpret the world.
Jean Piaget saw adaptation as two complementary processes: assimilation (fitting the world into existing schemas) and accommodation (changing schemas to fit the world).
Deferred imitation appears at the end of the sensorimotor stage and shows the child can hold a mental representation; operations first appear in the concrete operational stage.

wrong.1: Swaps (a) and (b): the logical-rules description belongs to operations, and copying absent models shows mental representation.
wrong.2: Only (c) is right; interpreting the world through current schemas is assimilation, not operations, and copying absent models is mental representation, not assimilation.
wrong.4: Every pair is wrong; for example, interpreting the world with current schemas is assimilation, not mental representation.

q: First make a small request; when the person complies, make another large request. This concept is based on which compliance technique?
who: Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser, foot-in-the-door

concept.t: The foot-in-the-door technique starts with a small request; once the person agrees, a larger related request is more likely to be accepted.
Agreeing to the small request changes how people see themselves (self-perception: 'I am the helpful type') and creates pressure to stay consistent.
Small then large = foot-in-the-door; refused large then smaller = door-in-the-face; good deal then added costs = lowball; extras added before a reply = that's-not-all.

wrong.2: Robert Cialdini's technique of starting with a large request that is refused, then a smaller one that seems a concession and invites reciprocity.
wrong.3: Wins agreement to an attractive deal, then raises the cost; people stick with their commitment even though the terms have worsened.
wrong.4: Jerry Burger's technique of sweetening the offer with a discount or extra item before the person has replied to the first offer.

q: When acetylcholine links up on the post-synaptic side, it generates a depolarisation. What do you call it?
doubt: An end plate potential is the neuromuscular form of an excitatory postsynaptic potential, so (2) is defensible if the stem means any ACh synapse.
who: End plate potential at the neuromuscular junction

concept.t: When acetylcholine from a motor neuron binds nicotinic receptors on the muscle's motor end plate, the resulting depolarisation is called the end plate potential (EPP).
ACh opens ligand-gated channels that let sodium in; the EPP is large enough to trigger a muscle action potential almost every time, and acetylcholinesterase then breaks ACh down.
EPP = depolarisation at a muscle fibre; EPSP = small graded depolarisation at a neuron; IPSP = hyperpolarisation.

wrong.1: A hyperpolarisation that makes the postsynaptic cell less likely to fire, so it cannot be the depolarisation described.
wrong.2: The general name for a small graded depolarisation at a neuron-to-neuron synapse; at the muscle, the depolarisation ACh produces is specifically the end plate potential.
wrong.4: Pairs a depolarisation with an IPSP, which is a hyperpolarisation; one event cannot be both.

q: The interaction of sensory impulses indicates the complexity of stimulation and therefore the difficulties in predicting behaviour. Behaviour is seldom a function of only one stimulus; rather it is a function of many stimuli. The above explanation is based on which learning theory?
who: Clark Hull, afferent neural interaction postulate

concept.t: The passage is Clark Hull's postulate on the interaction of sensory impulses (afferent neural interaction): stimuli arriving together modify one another, so behaviour reflects a pattern of many stimuli.
Hull built a hypothetico-deductive theory from formal postulates; its central ideas are drive reduction and habit strength, with reaction potential = habit strength × drive.
Hull = postulates and drive reduction; Edwin Guthrie = one-trial contiguity learning; Edward Tolman = cognitive maps and latent learning.

wrong.1: Contiguity theory: a stimulus pattern present during a movement will, on recurrence, produce that movement, learned in one trial; Edwin Guthrie set out no such postulate.
wrong.2: Classical conditioning pairs a conditioned stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus; Ivan Pavlov built no system of formal postulates about interacting sensory impulses.
wrong.4: Purposive behaviourism: learning through expectancies and cognitive maps, as Edward Tolman argued, not through interacting sensory impulses.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Psychologist): (a) Carol Ryff; (b) Seligman; (c) Viktor Frankl; (d) Suler 
 List-II (Concept): (i) Psychological well-being; (ii) Signature strength; (iii) Post-traumatic growth; (iv) Online disinhibition effect 
 Select the correct option:
who: Carol Ryff, Martin Seligman, Viktor Frankl, John Suler

concept.t: (a) Carol Ryff = (i) psychological well-being; (b) Martin Seligman = (ii) signature strengths; (c) Viktor Frankl = (iii) post-traumatic growth; (d) John Suler = (iv) online disinhibition effect.

Ryff's model has six dimensions of psychological well-being, including autonomy, purpose in life and self-acceptance; Seligman's signature strengths are a person's most characteristic character strengths.

Frankl, a concentration camp survivor, held that finding meaning in suffering lets people grow from trauma; Suler's online disinhibition effect explains why people say things online they would not say face to face.
The term post-traumatic growth was coined by Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun; Frankl's logotherapy is its forerunner.

wrong.2: Pairs Carol Ryff with signature strengths, which is Martin Seligman's idea; Ryff is known for the six-dimension model of psychological well-being.
wrong.3: Pairs Martin Seligman with psychological well-being (Ryff's model) and Viktor Frankl with online disinhibition, which is John Suler's idea.
wrong.4: Reverses every pair; for example, Carol Ryff did not study online disinhibition, which was described by John Suler.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Concept): (a) Big-C creativity; (b) Little-C creativity; (c) Mini-C creativity; (d) Pro-C creativity 
 List-II (Description): (i) Creativity of eminence; (ii) Creativity of everyday life recognised by others; (iii) Subjective and personal form of day-to-day creativity; (iv) Professional creativity which has not attained the status of eminence 
 Select the correct option:
who: James Kaufman and Ronald Beghetto, Four C model of creativity

concept.t: (a) Big-C = (i) creativity of eminence; (b) Little-c = (ii) everyday creativity recognised by others; (c) Mini-c = (iii) subjective, personal creativity; (d) Pro-c = (iv) professional creativity not yet eminent.
James Kaufman and Ronald Beghetto expanded the old Big-C and little-c split into a ladder: mini-c (personal insight while learning) → little-c (everyday) → Pro-c (expert) → Big-C (legendary).
Big-C examples are Einstein or Picasso; a student's idea that is new only to the student is mini-c.

wrong.2: Swaps Big-C with little-c and mini-c with Pro-c; Big-C is reserved for eminent, field-changing work.
wrong.3: Gives Big-C the subjective personal form, which is mini-c, and mini-c the eminent form, which is Big-C.
wrong.4: Reverses every pair; for example, Big-C is eminence, while professional creativity short of eminence is Pro-c.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Schools of Psychology): (a) Psychoanalysis; (b) Behaviourism; (c) Structuralism; (d) Transpersonal Psychology 
 List-II (Concept): (i) Elements of conscious experience; (ii) Self-actualization; (iii) Unconscious processes; (iv) S-R relations 
 Select the correct option:
who: Sigmund Freud, John Watson, Edward Titchener, Abraham Maslow

concept.t: (a) Psychoanalysis = (iii) unconscious processes; (b) Behaviourism = (iv) S-R relations; (c) Structuralism = (i) elements of conscious experience; (d) Transpersonal psychology = (ii) self-actualisation.

Sigmund Freud's psychoanalysis stresses unconscious motives; John B. Watson's behaviourism studies observable stimulus-response links; Edward Titchener's structuralism used introspection to find the elements of consciousness.
Abraham Maslow, a founder of transpersonal psychology (the 'fourth force'), extended self-actualisation to peak experiences and self-transcendence.

wrong.1: Swaps behaviourism and structuralism: Watson rejected consciousness and studied S-R links, while Titchener analysed the elements of conscious experience.
wrong.3: Gets only behaviourism right; it gives psychoanalysis Titchener's elements of consciousness and transpersonal psychology Freud's unconscious processes.
wrong.4: Every pair is wrong; for example, behaviourism concerns S-R relations, not self-actualisation, which belongs to humanistic and transpersonal psychology.

q:
Multiple sclerosis is: 
 
 (a) a demyelinating disorder

 (b) an autoimmune disease

 (c) always accompanied by amnesia and cognitive disorder

 (d) known to lead to jerky movements

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Multiple sclerosis, autoimmune demyelinating disease

concept.t: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks CNS myelin, leaving hardened scars (scleroses); damage to motor and cerebellar pathways causes tremor, ataxia and jerky movements.
Memory, attention and processing-speed problems affect many patients but not all, and severe amnesia is uncommon, so 'always' makes (c) false.
Jean-Martin Charcot's classic MS triad is nystagmus, intention tremor and scanning speech; symptoms often come and go in relapses and remissions.

wrong.1: True but incomplete: MS damage to motor and cerebellar pathways commonly produces tremor and ataxia, so (d) holds as well.
wrong.2: Includes (c), which is false: cognitive difficulties occur in many people with MS, but not always, and amnesia is not a defining feature.
wrong.4: Leaves out (b): MS is an autoimmune disease in which immune cells attack the myelin of the central nervous system.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): If children watch programmes with violent and aggressive content, they themselves take recourse to violent and aggressive behaviour. 
 Reason (R): Children learn aggressive behaviour from media through observational learning, where the observed behaviour need not be positively reinforced. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Albert Bandura, observational learning (Bobo doll studies)

concept.t: True as a general finding: children who watch violent content tend to behave more aggressively, as Albert Bandura's Bobo doll studies and later media-violence research show.
True, and it explains A: through observational learning children acquire behaviour simply by watching a model, with no reward needed for the child or the model.
Bandura separates learning from performance: seeing the model rewarded or punished affects whether the child performs the act, not whether it is learned.

wrong.2: (R) does explain (A): imitation through observational learning is the mechanism by which watched aggression becomes the child's own aggression.
wrong.3: (R) is true: Bandura showed children learn modelled aggression without any reinforcement for themselves or the model.
wrong.4: (A) is supported: children exposed to aggressive models, live or on screen, imitate the aggression, as the Bobo doll experiments showed.

q: Who proved the observation that cyclists seem to ride faster when they race against other cyclists than when they race alone?
who: Norman Triplett (1898), first social psychology experiment

concept.t: Norman Triplett noticed from cycling records that riders went faster when racing others than alone, and confirmed it in a lab study where children wound fishing reels faster in pairs.
This was the first demonstration of social facilitation: the presence of others, as co-actors or audience, improves performance on simple, well-learned tasks.
Triplett = first experiment in social psychology; Floyd Allport named social facilitation; Robert Zajonc explained it by arousal.

wrong.1: Later explained social facilitation by drive arousal: others' presence strengthens dominant responses, helping easy tasks and hurting hard ones.
wrong.2: Named social facilitation and studied co-acting groups about two decades later; Floyd Allport did not make the cyclist observation.
wrong.3: Proposed the distraction-conflict theory of social facilitation much later; Robert Baron did not make the original cyclist observation.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): The method of calculating IQ in terms of MA/CA x 100 as such does not work with adults. 
 Reason (R): Intelligence does not increase linearly with age past childhood. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: William Stern's ratio IQ versus David Wechsler's deviation IQ

concept.t: True. Ratio IQ (MA/CA × 100) breaks down for adults: a 40-year-old with a mental age of 20 would score 50 despite normal adult ability.
True, and it explains A: mental age stops rising steadily in the mid to late teens while chronological age keeps increasing, so the ratio falls artificially.
David Wechsler solved this with the deviation IQ, comparing a person with same-age peers (mean 100, SD 15).

wrong.2: (R) is the direct reason (A) holds: the formula assumes mental age rises in step with chronological age, which fails after childhood.
wrong.3: (R) is true: gains in mental age slow and level off after adolescence, so intelligence does not keep rising linearly with age.
wrong.4: (A) is true: dividing a levelled-off mental age by an ever-rising chronological age gives adults misleadingly low IQs.

q: A borrowed his father's car during a college vacation and smashed it after a party A attended. Expected reactions of his father run through A's mind and generate several possibilities. It is an example of which heuristic?
who: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, simulation heuristic

concept.t: A mentally runs through possible scenarios of how his father might react; judging outcomes by how easily they can be mentally simulated is the simulation heuristic.
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed that people build mental 'what if' scenarios; this underlies counterfactual thinking, such as stronger regret when a better outcome is easy to imagine.
Availability = how easily examples come to mind from memory; simulation = how easily a scenario can be constructed.

wrong.1: Judges frequency or probability by how easily past examples come to mind, not by imagining possible future scenarios.
wrong.2: Judges probability by how closely something resembles a typical case or prototype, often ignoring base rates.
wrong.3: Judging two events together as more likely than one alone, as in the Linda problem; it is a reasoning error, not a heuristic.

q: The cognitive approach to prejudice arises from which theory, that an individual's self-concept derives partly from membership in an in-group?
who: Henri Tajfel and John Turner, social identity theory (1979)

concept.t: Social identity theory says part of our self-concept comes from the groups we belong to. To feel good about ourselves we favour our in-group and look down on out-groups, which is the cognitive root of prejudice.
Three steps: social categorisation (sorting people into groups), social identification (taking the group into the self) and social comparison (rating our group above others).
Self-esteem from group membership = social identity; competition for scarce resources = realistic conflict; displaced frustration = scapegoat.

wrong.1: Muzafer Sherif's theory: prejudice grows from competition for scarce resources between groups, as in the Robbers Cave study, not from the self-concept.
wrong.2: Scapegoating means frustrated people displace hostility onto weaker, blameless groups; it is a motivational account of prejudice, not a self-concept one.
wrong.3: John Dollard and colleagues (1939) linked blocked goals to aggression; it explains hostility, not prejudice rooted in group-based identity.

q: Choose the correct answer for the leadership style: low task, low relationship style.
who: Paul Hersey and Ken Blanchard, situational leadership model

concept.t: In the situational leadership model, a leader who gives little direction (low task) and little support (low relationship) is delegating: the followers run the job themselves.
The right style depends on follower readiness (maturity). Low readiness needs direction; high readiness needs little of either.
S1 Telling = high task, low relationship; S2 Selling = high task, high relationship; S3 Participating = low task, high relationship; S4 Delegating = low task, low relationship.

wrong.1: This is S3: low task but high relationship; the leader shares decisions and supports followers who are able but unsure.
wrong.2: This is S2: high task and high relationship; the leader still directs but explains decisions and coaches.
wrong.4: This is S1: high task, low relationship; the leader gives clear instructions and supervises closely, for followers with low readiness.

q: Which of the following is a degenerative disease accompanied by amnesia, caused by frontotemporal lobular degeneration, and depression?
who: Arnold Pick; frontotemporal lobar degeneration

concept.t: Pick's disease is a form of frontotemporal lobar degeneration: the frontal and temporal lobes shrink and neurons fill with Pick bodies (tau protein).
Onset is usually in middle age. Personality change, disinhibition, apathy or depression-like withdrawal and language loss come first; memory loss follows.
Frontotemporal atrophy = Pick's; plaques and tangles with early memory loss = Alzheimer's; caudate loss with chorea = Huntington's; substantia nigra loss with tremor = Parkinson's.

wrong.1: Alzheimer's begins with memory loss from amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles, starting in the hippocampus and temporoparietal cortex, not focal frontotemporal lobar degeneration.
wrong.2: Parkinson's is loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra, causing resting tremor, rigidity and slow movement.
wrong.4: Huntington's is an inherited disorder with caudate and putamen loss, causing chorea, mood change and dementia.

q: Positive emotions are expressed as a result of activation of which of the following?
doubt: Some introductory texts simply say the left frontal lobe, so (3) is the runner-up; Richard Davidson's work places the activity in the left prefrontal cortex.
who: Richard Davidson, frontal asymmetry (approach-withdrawal) model

concept.t: EEG and imaging studies show more activity in the left prefrontal cortex during positive, approach-related emotions such as joy and interest.
In Richard Davidson's approach-withdrawal model, the left prefrontal area drives moving towards rewards, while the right prefrontal area drives withdrawal, as in fear, disgust and sadness.
Left prefrontal = positive mood and approach; right prefrontal = negative mood and withdrawal. People with more resting left-sided activity report more cheerful moods.

wrong.1: The right frontal areas are linked with negative, withdrawal-related emotions such as fear and sadness, not positive ones.
wrong.2: In Davidson's model the right prefrontal cortex serves withdrawal emotions; greater right activity goes with negative affect.
wrong.3: Correct hemisphere but too broad: the asymmetry is located in the prefrontal part of the left frontal lobe, not the frontal lobe as a whole.

q: Who has proposed a three-componential theory of wisdom explaining cognitive, affective and reflective wisdom?
who: Monika Ardelt, three-dimensional model of wisdom

concept.t: Monika Ardelt defined wisdom as a blend of three personality qualities, cognitive, reflective and affective, measured by her Three-Dimensional Wisdom Scale.
Cognitive: a wish to know the truth and understand life deeply. Reflective: seeing events from many angles, including oneself, without blame. Affective: sympathy and compassion for others.
Ardelt = three dimensions in the person; Baltes = Berlin wisdom paradigm (expert life knowledge); Sternberg = balance theory.

wrong.1: Robert Sternberg proposed the balance theory of wisdom: using knowledge to balance intrapersonal, interpersonal and extrapersonal interests for the common good.
wrong.2: Paul Baltes led the Berlin wisdom paradigm: wisdom as expert knowledge in the fundamental pragmatics of life, judged by five criteria.
wrong.3: Michael Chandler wrote about wisdom as a form of understanding beyond technical skill; the cognitive, reflective and affective model with its scale is Ardelt's.

q: A 12-year-old boy started showing a gradual onset of jerky, uncontrolled movements in the limbs with clumsiness, frequent falling, slurred speech and drooling, caused by HTT mutation. What disorder is he suffering from?
who: Juvenile Huntington's disease, HTT gene on chromosome 4

concept.t: The HTT gene makes the protein huntingtin. An expanded CAG repeat in it causes Huntington's disease; onset before 20 is called juvenile Huntington's.
Jerky, uncontrolled movements (chorea), clumsiness, falls, slurred speech and drooling, with later decline in thinking and mood. Juvenile cases often show more rigidity and seizures.
It is autosomal dominant: one faulty copy from either parent is enough. Neurons in the caudate and putamen die first.

wrong.1: Ataxia is loss of coordination, usually from cerebellar damage; it is a symptom with many causes, not the disorder an HTT mutation produces.
wrong.3: Dystonia is sustained, involuntary muscle contraction causing twisting postures; its genetic forms involve other genes such as DYT1, not HTT.
wrong.4: Essential tremor is a common, often familial action tremor of the hands and head, without chorea or an HTT mutation.

q: In Cattell's theory, the Dynamic Lattice shows the relationship among which of the following?
who: Raymond Cattell, dynamic lattice and subsidiation

concept.t: Raymond Cattell's dynamic lattice is a diagram of how attitudes serve sentiments, and sentiments in turn serve inborn ergs.
Ergs are innate drives (hunger, sex, curiosity). Sentiments are learned clusters of attitudes around objects such as career, home or self. Attitudes are specific interests in a course of action.
The chain is called subsidiation: an attitude is subsidiary to a sentiment, which is subsidiary to ergs. Liking a class serves a career sentiment, which serves security and self-assertion ergs.

wrong.1: Ability traits (how well a person copes) are a separate class of Cattell's traits; the lattice links only dynamic traits, so attitudes are missing.
wrong.2: Temperament traits (style of behaviour) are not part of the lattice, and sentiments, the link between ergs and attitudes, are left out.
wrong.3: Incomplete: the lattice starts from specific attitudes, which feed into sentiments and then into ergs.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Concept): (a) Savouring; (b) Hedonic adaptation; (c) Type-A behaviour; (d) Undoing hypothesis 
 List-II (Description): (i) Applying conscious awareness to enjoyment experiences; (ii) Happiness due to circumstances tends to be temporary; (iii) Hurry syndrome; (iv) Positive emotions lead to a quick recovery from detrimental effects 
 Select the correct option:
who: Bryant, Fredrickson, Friedman and Rosenman; positive and health psychology

concept.t: (a) Savouring = (i) applying conscious awareness to enjoyment; (b) Hedonic adaptation = (ii) happiness from circumstances is temporary; (c) Type-A behaviour = (iii) hurry syndrome; (d) Undoing hypothesis = (iv) positive emotions speed recovery.
Savouring (Fred Bryant) is deliberately noticing and prolonging good experiences. Hedonic adaptation is the hedonic treadmill: after a raise or a loss we drift back to our usual happiness level.

Type A (Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman) is time urgency, competitiveness and hostility. Barbara Fredrickson's undoing hypothesis says positive emotions undo the cardiovascular after-effects of negative ones.

wrong.2: Every pair is shifted: savouring is not temporary happiness, Type A is not conscious enjoyment, and the undoing hypothesis is not hurry syndrome.
wrong.3: Savouring is not hurry syndrome and Type A is not about recovery; hurry syndrome is the hallmark of Type A behaviour.
wrong.4: Reverses the list: quick recovery from negative states is the undoing hypothesis, and conscious enjoyment is savouring.

q: The major function of the parathyroid is to maintain the level of:
who: Parathyroid hormone (parathormone), calcium balance

concept.t: The four parathyroid glands behind the thyroid release parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium when it falls.
PTH frees calcium from bone, makes the kidneys keep calcium, and activates vitamin D so the gut absorbs more. Calcitonin from the thyroid works the other way.
Nerves and muscles need steady calcium. Too little causes tetany (muscle spasms); too much causes fatigue, depression and confusion.

wrong.2: Blood proteins such as albumin are made by the liver; the parathyroid does not regulate them.
wrong.3: PTH does switch on active vitamin D in the kidney, but only as a means of raising calcium; calcium is the level it maintains.
wrong.4: Glucocorticoids such as cortisol come from the adrenal cortex, under the control of ACTH from the pituitary.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): A 3- to 4-year-old will readily hand over a blanket to another individual who is rubbing hands and shivering a lot. 
 Reason (R): In sensitive face-to-face communication, infants connect emotionally with their caregivers; these experiences are believed to be the foundation for empathy. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: R describes the infant roots of empathy while A is a preschool act, so some would read R as true but not the explanation, which is (2).
who: Early development of empathy and prosocial behaviour

concept.t: True. By 2 to 4 years children show empathy and act on it: they comfort, share and hand things to someone who looks upset or cold. This is prosocial behaviour.
True. Warm face-to-face exchanges with caregivers teach babies to read and share another person's feelings, which is thought to lay the base for empathy.
R explains A: the emotional attunement built in infancy grows into empathy, and empathy is what moves the preschooler to help the shivering person.

wrong.2: R does more than sit beside A: it gives the developmental source of the empathy that drives the helping act in A.
wrong.3: R is true: sensitive early caregiving is widely seen as the root of empathy in developmental psychology.
wrong.4: A is true: preschoolers readily share and comfort when they see clear signs of distress such as shivering.

q: Repeated presentation of negative news in mass media may lead to an increase in the occurrence of such negative events because of:
doubt: If the item means copycat suicides after media reports, (1) Werther effect also fits, since it is the suicide form of the same contagion.
who: Media contagion (copycat) effect

concept.t: The contagion effect is the spread of a behaviour through exposure: heavy coverage of violence, riots, suicides or mass shootings is followed by a rise in similar acts.
Coverage offers models to imitate and makes the act seem common, in line with Albert Bandura's social learning and Robert Cialdini's social proof.
Contagion = any negative event copied after media exposure; Werther effect = copycat suicide only; Papageno effect = coping stories that reduce suicide.

wrong.1: David Phillips' term for the specific rise in suicides after publicised suicides; the stem speaks of negative events in general.
wrong.3: A learning and memory idea: items met more often are recognised and recalled more easily; it does not explain copied events.
wrong.4: Leo Crespi's finding that performance shifts sharply when the size of a reward is changed (contrast effect in rats), not media imitation.

q:
Marked impairments in establishing social interactions and living in their own world, repetitive behaviour patterns, and non-existent or poor language skills are three major characteristics of which disorder? 
 
 (a) Autism

 (b) Obsessive-compulsive disorder

 (c) Catatonic schizophrenia

 (d) Apraxia

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Leo Kanner, early infantile autism (1943)

concept.t: Poor social relating (living in their own world), repetitive, restricted behaviour and absent or delayed language are the classic triad of autism.
Leo Kanner described it in 1943. DSM-5 calls it autism spectrum disorder, with two domains: social communication deficits and restricted, repetitive behaviour.
Only (a) has all three features from early childhood. OCD and catatonia share some repetitive behaviour, and apraxia affects movement planning, but none shows this developmental picture.

wrong.2: OCD (b) has obsessions and compulsions with normal language; catatonic schizophrenia (c) shows stupor or posturing within psychosis, not a developmental triad.
wrong.3: Apraxia (d) is loss of skilled, purposeful movement despite intact strength, usually after brain damage; it is not a social or language disorder.
wrong.4: Autism (a) fits, but apraxia (d) is a motor planning disorder, so adding it makes the option wrong.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Psychologist): (a) Kelley; (b) Eysenck; (c) Cattell; (d) Hull 
 List-II (Concept): (i) Constructive alternativism; (ii) Hedonic tone; (iii) Hypothetico-deductive spiral; (iv) Response hierarchies 
 Select the correct option:
who: Kelly, Eysenck, Cattell and Hull; personality and learning theories

concept.t: (a) George Kelly = (i) constructive alternativism; (b) Hans Eysenck = (ii) hedonic tone; (c) Raymond Cattell = (iii) hypothetico-deductive spiral; (d) Clark Hull = (iv) response hierarchies.
Constructive alternativism: any event can be construed in many ways. Eysenck tied hedonic tone (how pleasant stimulation feels) to arousal: introverts reach their best level with less stimulation.
Cattell's inductive-hypothetico-deductive spiral cycles between data, hypotheses and testing. Hull's habit-family hierarchy ranks responses by habit strength, so the strongest appears first.

wrong.1: Swaps (b) and (c): the hypothetico-deductive spiral is Cattell's research method, and hedonic tone belongs to Eysenck's arousal theory.
wrong.2: Kelly's idea is constructive alternativism, not hedonic tone; response hierarchies are Hull's and the spiral is Cattell's.
wrong.4: Kelly's term is constructive alternativism and Eysenck's is hedonic tone; response hierarchies belong to Hull, not Cattell.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): Intelligent teachers select information that is relevant for their pedagogical purpose. 
 Reason (R): Selective combination involves determining which elements in a set of information are relevant for a given purpose. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Robert Sternberg and Janet Davidson, three processes of insight

concept.t: A is true, but R gives the wrong label. Picking out the relevant information is selective encoding, not selective combination.

Robert Sternberg's account: selective encoding = sifting relevant from irrelevant facts; selective combination = putting the chosen facts together into a whole; selective comparison = relating new information to old knowledge.
Encode = pick, combine = join, compare = link to the past. They are the knowledge-acquisition components of his triarchic theory.
