wrong.1: R is false as written, so it cannot explain A; the process in A is selective encoding.
wrong.2: R is not true: selective combination means joining relevant facts into a whole, not choosing which facts are relevant.
wrong.4: A is true: choosing information that suits the teaching goal is a mark of skilled, intelligent teaching.

q: Who gave the statement that the nature and frequency of human aggressive behaviour varies tremendously across human societies and is likely to occur in some more than others?
doubt: The line is the standard social-psychological critique of instinct theories rather than a famous quote; Leonard Berkowitz is the only option who rejected instinct views, with (3) a weak runner-up.
who: Leonard Berkowitz; social psychologists' critique of instinct theories

concept.t: Social psychologists such as Leonard Berkowitz argued that if aggression were an instinct it would look much the same everywhere. In fact its rate and form vary hugely between societies, which points to learning and situations.
Berkowitz's cognitive neoassociation model: unpleasant events create negative feeling that primes aggressive thoughts, and cues in the setting, such as weapons, make aggression more likely.
Instinct views: Sigmund Freud (Thanatos), Konrad Lorenz (fighting instinct). Cross-cultural variation is the classic argument against them.

wrong.2: Sigmund Freud saw aggression as an inborn death instinct (Thanatos) turned outward, so he expected it in all humans, not mainly in some societies.
wrong.3: John Dollard, Neal Miller and colleagues said frustration always leads to aggression; they stressed a universal frustration link, not variation across societies.
wrong.4: Konrad Lorenz, an ethologist, held that aggression is an innate fighting instinct that builds up and must be released, the view this statement argues against.

q: Which of the following is NOT true?
who: Broca's and Wernicke's areas; lateralisation and plasticity

concept.t: It is false because left frontal damage (Broca's area) mainly harms speech production. Comprehension problems come from left temporal damage (Wernicke's area).
Broca's aphasia: slow, effortful, telegraphic speech with fair understanding. Wernicke's aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech with poor understanding.
At birth the hemispheres have begun to specialise but are not fixed. Children with early left-hemisphere injury usually reach near-normal language because other areas take over, showing plasticity.

wrong.1: True: the newborn brain is only partly lateralised and highly plastic, which is why early injuries are recovered from better than later ones.
wrong.2: True: after early left-hemisphere damage, the right hemisphere or other left areas take over language, and children usually reach near-normal competence.
wrong.4: True: Broca's area in the left frontal lobe supports speech production and grammar, so damage gives halting, telegraphic speech.

q:
Fill in the blanks by choosing the right sequence. In the upside-down and reversed-image projection process on ______, the ______ bends the rays entering the eye and the light rays from the top of an object are projected onto ______ at the bottom of ______. 
 Select the correct option:
who: Image formation on the retina

concept.t: Retina, lens, receptors, retina: the image is projected upside down and reversed on the retina; the lens bends the light; rays from the top of an object land on receptors at the bottom of the retina.
The cornea and lens are curved, so light rays cross as they pass through. Top becomes bottom and left becomes right on the retina.
The brain interprets the inverted retinal image, so the world looks the right way up.

wrong.1: The image is projected on the retina, not on receptors, and the last two blanks give 'retina at the bottom of the retina', which makes no sense.
wrong.2: The lens bends light and the retina receives it; this order puts the lens where the image lands and the retina where the bending happens.
wrong.4: The last two blanks are reversed: rays land on receptors at the bottom of the retina, not on the retina at the bottom of the receptors.

q: Which of the following sequences of decision-making perspectives of prosocial behaviour is correct?
who: Bibb Latané and John Darley's decision model of helping

concept.t: Perceive a need → take personal responsibility → weigh costs and benefits → decide how to help → give help.
Help can fail at any step. If people miss the need, think someone else will act (diffusion of responsibility), or find the cost too high, no help is given.
It builds on Bibb Latané and John Darley's bystander research: notice, interpret as an emergency, assume responsibility, know how to help, then act.

wrong.2: Starts with responsibility and ends with perceived need; a person cannot take responsibility for a need they have not yet noticed.
wrong.3: Puts cost-benefit weighing first and responsibility last; responsibility comes right after the need is perceived, and help comes last.
wrong.4: Places responsibility after deciding how to help; first one accepts responsibility, then weighs costs and chooses the form of help.

q: When people are pressurized to admit guilt but privately continue to believe in their own innocence, this is the correct answer for the above statement:
who: Saul Kassin and Lawrence Wrightsman, types of false confession

concept.t: In a coerced-compliant false confession the suspect gives in to pressure (to end questioning, avoid threats or gain a promise) but privately still knows they are innocent.

Voluntary: confessing with no police pressure, for attention or to protect someone. Coerced-compliant: public compliance, private belief in innocence. Coerced-internalised: the suspect comes to believe they did it.
Compliance = says it, does not believe it. Internalisation = says it and believes it.

wrong.1: A voluntary false confession is given without police pressure, for example to seek attention or protect the real offender.
wrong.3: Here the suspect, worn down by tactics such as false evidence, comes to believe they are guilty; in the stem belief in innocence remains.
wrong.4: Character evidence is testimony about a person's general traits or reputation, used to suggest how they acted; it is not a type of confession.

q: Torrance used the term 'creatively handicapped' for whom?
doubt: This is a niche Torrance term; the runner-up is (2), the high-IQ, low-creativity group, which some might read as lacking in creativity.
who: E. Paul Torrance, studies of creative children

concept.t: E. Paul Torrance noted that highly creative children often do not fit school routines, so they underachieve and are seen as difficult. He called them creatively handicapped: their creativity becomes a handicap in a conformist classroom.
Schools reward memory and convergent thinking, while these children excel at divergent thinking. Without support they may hide or give up their creativity.
Torrance also built the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT), scored for fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration.

wrong.2: The bright, conforming student who does well in school; Jacob Getzels and Philip Jackson contrasted this group with high-creative students.
wrong.3: Students average on both measures fit ordinary school demands and are not singled out by any special label.
wrong.4: Students struggling on both counts; the term described creativity causing school problems, not a lack of creativity.

q: Hold a pencil at arm's length and look at it first with one eye then with the other. There is a little difference between the two views relative to the background. Now bring the pencil just six inches away from your face and try the same thing. This time you will perceive a great difference between the two views. Which one is the correct answer for the above example?
who: Binocular (retinal) disparity

concept.t: Each eye sees the pencil from a slightly different angle. This binocular disparity needs both eyes, so it is a binocular cue to depth.
The closer the object, the bigger the difference between the two retinal images. The brain reads a large disparity as near and a small one as far.
Binocular cues: retinal disparity and convergence. Monocular cues: linear perspective, interposition, texture gradient, relative size, motion parallax.

wrong.1: Depth cues such as interposition or linear perspective that work with one eye; this demonstration depends on comparing the views of two eyes.
wrong.3: Using knowledge and expectation to interpret input; the demonstration shows a raw sensory cue from two eyes.
wrong.4: Building perception up from sensory data; it is a general processing mode, not the specific depth cue shown here.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): Mental stress may cause cardiac ischemia. 
 Reason (R): Stress unfavorably affects the balance between cardiac demand and supply. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
who: Mental stress-induced myocardial ischaemia

concept.t: True. Myocardial ischaemia means the heart muscle gets too little blood and oxygen. Acute mental stress can trigger it, especially in people with coronary artery disease.
True. Stress hormones raise heart rate and blood pressure, which increases the heart's oxygen demand, while coronary vessels may constrict and cut supply.
R explains A: ischaemia is exactly a mismatch in which demand exceeds supply.

wrong.2: R is the mechanism behind A, not a separate fact: stress upsets demand and supply, and that mismatch is ischaemia.
wrong.3: R is true: stress raises demand through heart rate and blood pressure and can reduce supply through coronary constriction.
wrong.4: A is true: mental stress-induced ischaemia is well documented in coronary patients, often without chest pain.

q: Which attention is shifted without moving the eyes, commonly referred to as seeing something out of the corner of one's eye?
who: Michael Posner, covert orienting of attention

concept.t: Covert attention shifts focus to a location without moving the eyes, as when you notice something out of the corner of your eye.
In Michael Posner's cueing task, people respond faster to targets at a cued spot even with their eyes fixed on the centre, showing attention moved covertly.
Covert = attention moves, eyes stay; overt = eyes and head turn to the target.

wrong.2: Overt attention means moving the eyes or head to look straight at the object of interest.
wrong.3: Divided attention is splitting attention between two or more tasks at once, such as driving while talking.
wrong.4: Span of attention is the number of items a person can grasp in a single brief exposure.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Type of skin receptors): (a) Meissner's corpuscles; (b) Pacinian corpuscles; (c) Krause's end bulbs; (d) Free nerve endings 
 List-II (Sensory function): (i) cold; (ii) pain; (iii) touch; (iv) pressure 
 Select the correct option:
who: Cutaneous receptors, classic skin-senses account

concept.t: (a) Meissner's corpuscles = (iii) touch; (b) Pacinian corpuscles = (iv) pressure; (c) Krause's end bulbs = (i) cold; (d) Free nerve endings = (ii) pain.
Meissner's corpuscles lie just under the skin surface and sense light touch. Pacinian corpuscles are deep, onion-like and respond to pressure and vibration.
Classic texts link Krause's end bulbs with cold and Ruffini endings with warmth. Free nerve endings carry pain and temperature.

wrong.1: Meissner's corpuscles sense light touch, not pain; pain is carried by free nerve endings, and Krause's end bulbs are linked with cold.
wrong.3: Pacinian corpuscles respond to pressure and vibration, not cold, and Meissner's corpuscles serve touch, not pressure.
wrong.4: Pacinian corpuscles do not carry pain, and free nerve endings are chiefly pain receptors, not cold ones; Meissner's serve touch.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): According to Freud, painful memories are the target of repression. 
 Reason (R): Repression can be primal, i.e. innately part of the Id, or proper, i.e. an unacceptable derivative of original Id impulses. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: If R is read as saying why painful material is pushed out, some would choose (1), but R only classifies the kinds of repression.
who: Sigmund Freud, primal repression and repression proper

concept.t: True. For Sigmund Freud, repression pushes threatening, painful memories, wishes and impulses out of consciousness into the unconscious.
True. Freud split it into primal repression, which keeps id impulses from ever reaching awareness, and repression proper, which pushes out later ideas and memories linked to those impulses.
R lists two kinds of repression; it does not say why painful memories are its target. The reason is anxiety: repression protects the ego from it.

wrong.1: R only classifies repression into two kinds; the reason painful memories are repressed is that they arouse anxiety, which R does not mention.
wrong.3: R is true: Freud did distinguish primal repression from repression proper, the after-pressure on derivatives of the original impulse.
wrong.4: A is true: Freud saw repression as the basic defence that keeps painful and threatening memories out of awareness.

q:
The mechanistic view of motivation can be characterised by which of the following? 
 
 (a) S-O-R

 (b) Direction is determined by S-R bonds

 (c) Probability of habits depends on prior reinforcement contingencies

 (d) Persistence of behaviour

 
 Select the correct option:
doubt: Clark Hull's theory has intervening organism variables and is sometimes written as S-O-R, which would give (1); but S-O-R usually marks the cognitive, purposive view.
who: Clark Hull's drive theory, mechanistic view of motivation

concept.t: The mechanistic view treats motivated behaviour as automatic: S-R bonds (habits) set its direction, past reinforcement sets how likely each habit is, and behaviour persists while the sustaining stimuli last.
In Clark Hull's drive theory, a need creates drive, which energises whatever habits the situation calls up. No conscious intention or goal is assumed.
S-O-R places the organism's inner states, expectancies and goals between stimulus and response. That mediating role is the mark of the cognitive view, as in Edward Tolman's purposive behaviourism.
Mechanistic = automatic push (drive, habit, reinforcement); cognitive = conscious pull (expectancy, value, goals).

wrong.1: Brings in (a), the S-O-R formula with mediating goals and expectancies, which belongs to the cognitive view, and drops (d), the mechanistic account of persistence.
wrong.2: Brings in (a), the cognitive S-O-R formula, and drops (c), although habit strength built by past reinforcement is central to Hull's mechanistic theory.
wrong.4: Cannot be right because (a), with its mediating organism variables such as goals and expectancies, describes the cognitive view rather than the mechanistic one.

q: Which of the following endeavours to revalue the unique qualities associated with womanhood and femininity?
who: Cultural (difference) feminism

concept.t: Cultural feminism holds that women have distinct qualities, such as care, nurturance and cooperation, that society undervalues. It seeks to revalue these qualities rather than erase gender differences.
It is a form of difference feminism: the goal is not to make women like men but to honour a female way of being and relating.
Liberal = equal rights and access; radical = patriarchy is the root; socialist = capitalism plus patriarchy; cultural = celebrate femininity.

wrong.2: Liberal feminism seeks equal legal rights, education and opportunity for women within existing institutions, stressing sameness with men, not special feminine qualities.
wrong.3: Radical feminism sees patriarchy and male control of women's bodies and sexuality as the root of oppression and calls for overturning the gender system.
wrong.4: Socialist feminism links women's oppression to both capitalism and patriarchy, focusing on class and unpaid domestic labour.

q:
The Mayer-Salovey-Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test (MSCEIT) measures which of the following? 
 
 (a) Perceiving emotions

 (b) Using emotions to facilitate thought

 (c) Understanding emotions

 (d) Self-motivation

 
 Select the correct option:
who: John Mayer, Peter Salovey, David Caruso: four-branch ability model

concept.t: The MSCEIT is an ability test built on the four-branch model of John Mayer and Peter Salovey. Perceiving, using and understanding emotions are three of its branches; self-motivation is not.
(1) Perceiving emotions in faces and pictures; (2) using emotions to facilitate thought; (3) understanding how emotions blend and change; (4) managing emotions in self and others.
Self-motivation comes from Daniel Goleman's mixed model (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills), not from the ability model.

wrong.1: Leaves out (c) understanding emotions, which is the third branch of the four-branch ability model that the MSCEIT measures.
wrong.2: Includes (d) self-motivation, which belongs to Daniel Goleman's mixed model, and leaves out perceiving emotions, the first MSCEIT branch.
wrong.4: Includes (d) self-motivation from Goleman's model and drops (a) perceiving emotions, the most basic MSCEIT branch.

q: The quotation, "People believe good things should happen to good people and bad things to bad people" represents:
who: Melvin Lerner, belief in a just world

concept.t: The just-world hypothesis of Melvin Lerner says people need to believe the world is fair, so good people are rewarded and bad people get what they deserve.
To protect this belief, people often blame the victim, for example assuming a victim of crime or illness must have done something to deserve it.
Just-world belief → victim derogation; it is a motivated belief that keeps the world feeling predictable and safe.

wrong.1: Not a recognised theory of fairness beliefs; the idea that good things happen to good people is Lerner's just-world belief.
wrong.3: Karma is a religious and philosophical doctrine of moral cause and effect across lives, not the social psychology term for this belief.
wrong.4: Retribution means deserved punishment for wrongdoing; it is not the named social psychology hypothesis about believing the world is fair.

q: An observer watches a video in which the speaker's lips form the sound 'ga-ga' while the sound track provides speech that is normally perceived as 'ba-ba'. The conjunction of these conflicting sources produces the perception of 'da-da', which integrates this information and results in which illusion?
who: Harry McGurk and John MacDonald, McGurk effect (1976)

concept.t: Seeing lips say 'ga' while hearing 'ba' makes people hear 'da'. This is the McGurk effect, a cross-modal illusion, because vision changes what is heard.
The brain fuses auditory and visual speech cues into one best guess; 'da' is a compromise between the lip movement of 'ga' and the sound of 'ba'.
McGurk effect = audiovisual speech; ventriloquism effect = sound location pulled toward the seen source. Both show multisensory integration.

wrong.2: Size illusions, such as the Ponzo or Ebbinghaus illusion, distort perceived size within vision alone and involve no sound.
wrong.3: The Müller-Lyer illusion makes two equal lines look unequal because of arrow-like fins; it is purely visual.
wrong.4: A visual illusion stays within one sense; here vision alters hearing, so the illusion crosses two modalities.

q:
Retrieval is more commonly explained as the basis of which generation-recognition theory? 
 
 (a) Information Processing

 (b) Iconic Image

 (c) Sensory Register

 (d) Primacy Effect

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Generate-recognise (two-stage) theory of recall

concept.t: The generate-recognise theory explains retrieval as an information-processing sequence: first generate candidate items from memory, then run a recognition check on each.
Recall needs both stages, while recognition needs only the second. This explains why recognition is usually easier than recall.
Linked to John Anderson and Gordon Bower, and to Walter Kintsch; Endel Tulving's recognition failure of recallable words later challenged it.

wrong.1: Adds (b) and (c): the iconic image and sensory register are the brief sensory store at input, not retrieval processes.
wrong.3: The iconic image and sensory register belong to sensory memory, which holds raw input for under a second; they play no part in retrieval theory.
wrong.4: The iconic image is visual sensory memory and the primacy effect is better recall of early list items; neither is the basis of generate-recognise theory.

q: Which of the following is the correct explanation of the outgroup homogeneity effect?
who: Outgroup homogeneity effect, social categorisation

concept.t: The outgroup homogeneity effect is seeing outgroup members as all alike ('they are all the same') while seeing one's own group as varied.
We know many in-group members as individuals and meet outgroup members less, so we hold a simpler, more stereotyped picture of them.
Outgroup homogeneity → 'they are all alike'; in-group bias → favouring 'us'; minimal group paradigm → Henri Tajfel's arbitrary groups.

wrong.1: This describes assumed similarity within the in-group, close to the false consensus effect, not the perceived sameness of outgroup members.
wrong.3: This reverses in-group favouritism; people normally give more favourable evaluations and rewards to their own group, not the outgroup.
wrong.4: This describes Henri Tajfel's minimal group paradigm, the method that showed in-group bias even with trivial, arbitrary groups.

q: Which of the following sequences of Bandura's observational learning is correct?
who: Albert Bandura, observational learning (1977)

concept.t: Albert Bandura: attention (notice the model) → retention (store it as images or words) → production (reproduce the act) → motivation (a reason to perform it).
You cannot store what you did not notice or copy what you did not store; motivation then decides whether the learned behaviour is shown.
The Bobo doll studies showed learning without performance: children who had seen the model punished imitated more once rewards were offered.

wrong.2: Puts retention before attention, but a model's behaviour must be noticed before it can be stored in memory.
wrong.3: Puts motivation second; motivation governs whether already learned behaviour is performed, so it comes last.
wrong.4: Swaps the last two steps; motivation is the final step that decides whether the reproduced behaviour is actually shown.

q: Projective measures, particularly inkblot tests, index which of the following?
doubt: The source of this classification is unclear; inkblot responses are also scored for originality, which would point to novelty (1).
who: Creativity assessment: inkblots as meaning-making tasks

concept.t: Inkblots have no fixed content, so the person must assign meaning to an ambiguous shape. Creativity then shows as rich, apt interpretations, that is, creativity in a meaning context.
This is like the pattern meanings and line meanings tasks of Michael Wallach and Nathan Kogan, where children say what abstract drawings could be.
Divergent-thinking tests stress fluency and originality; expert ratings of products tap domain-specific creativity; self-report checklists tap everyday creativity.

wrong.1: Novelty is indexed mainly by originality scores on divergent-thinking tasks such as unusual uses; inkblots ask the person to interpret, that is, to make meaning.
wrong.3: Domain-specific creativity is judged from real products in one field, such as poems or collages, rated by experts, as in Teresa Amabile's consensual assessment technique.
wrong.4: Everyday (little-c) creativity is measured by self-report checklists of creative acts in daily life, not by responses to ambiguous inkblots.

q:
Which of the following theorists used the idiographic approach to personality? 
 
 (a) Allport

 (b) Kelley

 (c) Cattell

 (d) Eysenck

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Gordon Allport and George Kelly, idiographic approach

concept.t: Gordon Allport championed the idiographic study of the unique person (as in his Letters from Jenny), and George Kelly (printed 'Kelley') mapped each person's own constructs with the Rep test.
Idiographic = in-depth study of one person's unique pattern; nomothetic = general laws and traits measured across many people.
Raymond Cattell (16PF) and Hans Eysenck (PEN model) were nomothetic factor analysts; Allport brought the idiographic and nomothetic terms into psychology.

wrong.2: Adds Raymond Cattell, whose 16PF trait model came from factor analysis of large samples, a nomothetic approach.
wrong.3: Cattell and Hans Eysenck both used factor analysis to find traits common to everyone, the nomothetic approach, not the idiographic one.
wrong.4: Adds Cattell and Eysenck, both nomothetic factor analysts, and leaves out George Kelly, whose Rep test maps each person's own constructs.

q:
Match List-I with List-II: 
 List-I (Concept): (a) Impairment; (b) Disability; (c) Handicap; (d) Disadvantage 
 List-II (Description): (i) Any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological or anatomical structure or function; (ii) Any restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in an age-appropriate manner; (iii) Perception and assessment of one's abilities to be lower relative to others; (iv) Inability to perform within expected norms 
 Select the correct option:
who: WHO International Classification of Impairments, Disabilities and Handicaps (1980)

concept.t: (a) Impairment = (i) loss or abnormality of structure or function; (b) Disability = (ii) restricted ability to perform an activity; (c) Handicap = (iii) judged lower relative to others; (d) Disadvantage = (iv) inability to perform within expected norms.
The WHO ICIDH chain runs impairment (body level) → disability (activity level) → handicap (social disadvantage in fulfilling a normal role).
Loss of a leg is an impairment, being unable to walk is a disability, and losing a job because of it is a handicap.
Only option 1 pairs impairment with (i) and disability with (ii), the textbook WHO definitions, so the remaining pairs follow.

wrong.2: Gives impairment the 'restriction of activity' description, which is the WHO definition of disability, not impairment.
wrong.3: Gives impairment the 'lower relative to others' description; impairment is the loss or abnormality of structure or function itself.
wrong.4: Matches impairment with 'inability to perform within norms'; WHO defines impairment at the level of body structure or function.

q: According to Jung, what is made up of all the archetypes taken together?
who: Carl Jung, analytical psychology

concept.t: For Carl Jung, the collective unconscious is the inherited layer of the psyche shared by all humans, and its contents are the archetypes.
Archetypes are universal, inborn patterns, such as the persona, shadow, anima and animus, and the self, that appear in myths, dreams and religions.
Personal unconscious holds complexes; collective unconscious holds archetypes.

wrong.1: Jung's personal unconscious holds an individual's forgotten and repressed experiences, organised into complexes, not the inherited archetypes.
wrong.3: The mandala is a circular symbol of wholeness that expresses the self archetype; it is one symbol, not the sum of all archetypes.
wrong.4: The shadow is a single archetype: the dark, unacceptable, animal side of the personality.

q:
Which of the following are steps of the problem-solving cycle? 
 
 (a) Problem identification

 (b) Problem definition

 (c) Organization

 (d) Allocation of resources

 
 Select the correct option:
who: Robert Sternberg, problem-solving cycle

concept.t: Robert Sternberg's problem-solving cycle includes all four: identify the problem, define it, organise the information, and allocate resources.
Problem identification → problem definition → strategy formulation → organisation of information → allocation of resources → monitoring → evaluation.
It is a cycle because solving one problem often reveals a new one, which restarts identification.

wrong.1: Covers only the first two steps; organising information and allocating resources are also steps in Sternberg's cycle.
wrong.2: Leaves out problem identification and definition, which open the cycle and must come before any organising.
wrong.3: Leaves out problem identification, the first step: a problem must be recognised before it can be defined.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): The likelihood that fetal alcohol syndrome will occur depends on the social environment. 
 Reason (R): Social influences also act upon the developing brain and mind. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: One can argue that poverty acts through drinking patterns and nutrition rather than through social influence on the brain, which would give (2).
who: Prenatal development in social context (biocultural view)

concept.t: True. Fetal alcohol syndrome is far more common among poor mothers: poor nutrition, stress, heavier drinking and little prenatal care all raise the risk.
True. Development is biocultural: social conditions reach the fetus and the developing brain through the mother's body, diet and behaviour.
R explains A: because social influences act on the developing brain, the same teratogen (alcohol) has different effects in different social settings.
A teratogen's harm depends on dose, timing (critical periods), genes and the environment.

wrong.2: R is not a side fact: it is the principle that makes A true, since social conditions shape how alcohol affects prenatal brain growth.
wrong.3: R is true; prenatal and early brain development are shaped by social factors such as poverty, nutrition and maternal stress.
wrong.4: A is true: the risk of fetal alcohol syndrome rises with poverty and poor nutrition, so its likelihood does depend on the social environment.

q:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Read the statements. 
 Assertion (A): Changing a client's perception requires persuasive skills and direction from the counsellor, and such input is known as a lead. 
 Reason (R): The counsellor should make minimum verbal responses and maintain silence so that clients feel some pressure to continue, and will choose to continue with minimum input from the counsellor, thus the counsellor taking a good lead. 
 Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
doubt: R uses 'lead' loosely; if minimal responses are judged not to be a lead at all, R is false and the answer is (3).
who: Counselling leads and minimal encouragers

concept.t: True. A lead is a counsellor response that directs the client's thinking; changing a client's perception calls for strong leads such as interpretation, confrontation and persuasion.
True. Minimal encouragers ('mm-hmm', a nod) and silence are the weakest leads: they put gentle pressure on the client to keep talking with little counsellor input.
R does not explain A: A is about strong, directive leads that change perceptions, while R describes minimal leads that only keep the client talking.
Leads run on a continuum from silence (least lead) through restatement and questions to interpretation and advice (most lead).

wrong.1: Both are true, but R describes minimal leads that keep the client talking, not the persuasive direction needed to change perceptions in A.
wrong.3: R is true: minimal verbal responses and silence are recognised low-level leads that encourage the client to continue.
wrong.4: A is true: directive responses that steer a client's thinking, including persuasion, are what counselling texts call leads.

q:
Read the following paragraph and answer the five questions which follow. A psychologist wanted to develop an achievement test in Chemistry for SSC students of central schools. For this purpose he wrote 110 items having a multiple-choice format and administered this draft version to a sample of 300 subjects. Item analysis was carried out by computing item-remainder correlations, and retained 80 items. The eighty-item version was administered to a fresh sample of 400 subjects, which yielded a mean of 40.00 and a standard deviation of 8.00. The scores were found to be normally distributed. Cronbach's alpha for the eighty-item version was found to be 0.94. The psychologist also computed odd-even reliability and Kuder-Richardson (K-R) reliability for this version. On this version, one of the subjects, Manas, had a score of 32. Since the eighty-item version was considered long for administration, two forms, Form A and Form B, were prepared by randomly assigning 40 items to each form. 
 The expected Cronbach's alpha for Form A would be:
who: Spearman-Brown prophecy formula

concept.t: Form A has 40 of the 80 items, half the length. The Spearman-Brown formula predicts the reliability of a test whose length changes by a factor n.
Halving a test lowers reliability but does not halve it; 0.47 is the trap. Lengthening raises reliability with diminishing returns.

wrong.1: Simply halves 0.94; reliability does not fall in proportion to length, as the Spearman-Brown formula shows.
wrong.3: Too low; starting from an alpha of 0.94, a half-length test keeps reliability near 0.89 by the Spearman-Brown formula.
wrong.4: That is the alpha of the full 80-item test; removing half the items must lower reliability.

q:
In the above study, the psychologist computed three reliability coefficients: 
 
 (a) Cronbach's alpha

 (b) Split-half reliability coefficient

 (c) Kuder-Richardson (K-R) reliability coefficient

 
 Which one of the following expectations is true?
who: Lee Cronbach's alpha and Kuder-Richardson KR-20

concept.t: Multiple-choice items scored right or wrong are dichotomous, and for such items Cronbach's alpha and KR-20 are the same formula, so (a) and (c) match.
Split-half (odd-even) reliability rests on one particular split and then needs the Spearman-Brown correction, so it can be higher or lower than alpha.
Lee Cronbach showed alpha is the average of all possible split-half coefficients, so any single split can come out different.

wrong.1: Split-half depends on how the items are split and so can differ from alpha; only alpha and KR-20 are identical for dichotomous items.
wrong.3: Split-half and K-R are computed differently and need not agree; it is alpha and K-R that coincide for right or wrong items.
wrong.4: Alpha and KR-20 cannot differ here: KR-20 is the special case of alpha for items scored 0 or 1.

q: For computing item-remainder correlations, which one of the following correlations would be suitable?
who: Point-biserial correlation in item analysis

concept.t: An item-remainder correlation links one item scored 0 or 1 (a true dichotomy) with the total on the remaining items (continuous). The point-biserial r is built for exactly this pairing.
Leaving the item out of the total stops the correlation being inflated by the item correlating with itself.
Dichotomous + continuous = point-biserial (biserial if the dichotomy is artificial); two dichotomies = phi or tetrachoric.

wrong.1: Phi is for two genuinely dichotomous variables, such as two items scored right or wrong, not an item paired with a continuous total.
wrong.2: The contingency coefficient measures association between two nominal variables in a cross-table, based on chi-square.
wrong.4: Tetrachoric r is for two variables that are both artificially dichotomised from underlying normal distributions.

q: The score of 32 (score obtained by Manas on the eighty-item version) would correspond to percentile rank:
who: Normal curve: z score to percentile rank

concept.t: z = (X - M) / SD = (32 - 40) / 8 = -1.00. About 15.87% of a normal distribution lies below z = -1, so the percentile rank is about 16.
34.13% of cases lie between the mean and 1 SD, so 50 - 34.13 = 15.87% lie more than one SD below the mean.
Remember 16, 50, 84 for z = -1, 0, +1, and about 2 and 98 for z = -2 and +2.

wrong.2: 32 is Manas's raw score, not his relative standing; a raw score is not a percentile rank.
wrong.3: 80 is the number of items on the test, not the percentage of people scoring below 32.
wrong.4: 84 is the percentile for z = +1, a score of 48; Manas is one SD below the mean, not above it.

q: The 95% confidence interval for the true score of 32 would be:
who: Standard error of measurement, confidence interval

concept.t: The standard error of measurement is the spread of a person's observed scores around their true score over many hypothetical retests.
68% interval = ±1 SEM; 95% = ±1.96 SEM; 99% = ±2.58 SEM. Higher reliability gives a narrower band.

wrong.1: 0.94 is the reliability coefficient itself, not a band in score units; the band must come from the SEM.
wrong.2: This band is one SEM wide, which gives only about a 68% interval; 95% needs 1.96 × SEM = 3.84.
wrong.3: Too wide; with an SD of 8 and reliability of 0.94, the 95% band is 1.96 × 1.96 = 3.84 points.

q:
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow. A researcher wanted to study the effect of organization of material (A) on recall. She expected that retention interval (B) would moderate the effect of organization of material. She varied A at three levels (low organization, moderate organization, and high organization) and varied B at two levels (short retention interval and long retention interval). The subjects were randomly assigned to the different groups. Each subject received the list of words with the specified level of organization, learnt the list up to one errorless trial, and was tested after the specified retention interval. All the subjects had also received an intelligence test. The number of items recalled by the subject was the dependent variable. The data were analysed by the appropriate ANOVA, treating intelligence as a covariate. The partial results are: (i) the sum of squares for organization of material (A) was 255.00; (ii) the degrees of freedom for error variance was 115; (iii) the F ratio for interaction (A x B) was 0.95. The obtained results were appropriately interpreted. 
 The design in the above study can be best labelled as:
who: Factorial ANCOVA design with unequal cell sizes

concept.t: Two factors are crossed (A: 3 levels × B: 2 levels), subjects are randomly assigned, and intelligence is a covariate. Error df = N - 6 - 1 = 115 gives N = 122, which cannot split equally into 6 cells, so the design is unbalanced.
Balanced = equal n in every cell; unbalanced = unequal cell sizes, so the effects are no longer independent and need adjusted sums of squares.
Moderation (B changing the effect of A) can only be tested in a factorial design, through the A × B interaction.

wrong.1: Calling it single-factor hides the two crossed factors; a factorial design is needed to test whether retention interval moderates organisation.
wrong.2: Balanced needs equal cells, but 122 subjects cannot be divided equally among 6 groups (122 / 6 is not a whole number).
wrong.4: Blocking groups subjects on a variable before assignment; here intelligence is a covariate adjusted statistically, and subjects were simply randomised.

q: The mean square for organization of material would be:
who: Mean square = sum of squares / df

concept.t: MS = SS / df. Organisation of material has 3 levels, so df = 3 - 1 = 2, and MS = 255.00 / 2 = 127.50.
df for a factor = levels - 1; df for an interaction = product of the factors' df (here 2 × 1 = 2).

wrong.1: Divides by 6, the number of cells; a main effect's sum of squares is divided by its own df (levels - 1).
wrong.3: Divides by 3, the number of levels, instead of the degrees of freedom (3 - 1 = 2).
wrong.4: This is the sum of squares itself; it would equal the mean square only if df were 1.

q: From the above results, it can be concluded that:
who: Interpreting F ratios in factorial ANCOVA

concept.t: The A × B F ratio is 0.95, below 1, so it cannot be significant. The interaction is the test of moderation, so retention interval does not moderate the effect of organisation.
MS for organisation is known (127.50) but MS error is not given, so its F ratio cannot be computed and no conclusion is possible.
An F below 1 is never significant, because the effect variance is smaller than the error variance.

wrong.1: Cannot be judged: MS error is not given, so the F ratio for organisation of material cannot be computed.
wrong.2: Equally untestable: without MS error there is no F ratio for organisation and no basis to call it non-significant.
wrong.4: Moderation would need a significant A × B interaction, but F = 0.95 is below 1 and cannot be significant.

q: How many subjects have been employed in this study?
who: ANCOVA error degrees of freedom

concept.t: Total df (N - 1) splits into between cells (6 - 1 = 5), covariate (1) and error. So error df = N - 6 - 1; 115 = N - 7, giving N = 122.
In ANCOVA each covariate takes 1 df from the error term, so error df = N - number of cells - number of covariates.

wrong.1: 116 is error df + 1, which ignores the 5 df used by the cells and the 1 df used by the covariate.
wrong.2: 120 assumes 20 per cell, but that would give error df = 120 - 6 - 1 = 113, not 115.
wrong.3: 121 forgets the covariate's 1 df; with a covariate, error df = N - 6 - 1.

q: What would be the degrees of freedom for the covariate?
who: ANCOVA: one df per covariate

concept.t: Each covariate is one continuous predictor with one regression slope, so it uses exactly 1 df. Intelligence is the only covariate here.
ANCOVA removes the variance in recall predicted by intelligence, then tests A, B and A × B on the adjusted scores.
df for k covariates = k, and they come out of the error df.

wrong.2: 2 is the df for organisation of material (3 levels - 1) and for the A × B interaction, not for a single covariate.
wrong.3: 5 is the between-cells df (6 groups - 1), not the df for the covariate.
wrong.4: 6 is the number of groups in the 3 × 2 design, not a degrees-of-freedom value.
